body_markdown:
After a five-year global hiatus, the Mitsubishi Pajero is back—and it looks quite competent. Last night, Mitsubishi debuted an all-new generation of the company’s fabled cross-country SUV, the fifth iteration of the nameplate since 1982.


Mitsubishi


We’ll cut right to the chase: There’s no word yet on whether the Pajero will reach U.S. shores. We haven’t had a Pajero (called the[Montero](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/next-mitsubishi-montero-debut-date/) here) stateside since 2006, and that’s a bit of a bummer. In its heyday, the[Montero was an extremely viable alternative](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/mitsubishis-second-gen-montero-isnt-collector-grade-yet-but-thats-a-good-thing/) to the Toyota Land Cruisers, Jeep Wagoneers, and Land Rovers of the world. (Your author happens to be the current caretaker of a[1998 Montero](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/montero-in-moab-growing-to-love-an-overlooked-4x4-in-the-age-of-escape/) , and he adores it.)


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi’s engineers didn’t mess around with the big three-row ute. The tri-diamond brand wants the new Pajero to act as a flagship of sorts for the company, which means everything about it needs to be the best that Mitsubishi can offer.


Mitsubishi


Pajeros have always been known for their[off-road capability](https://www.hagerty.com/media/buying-and-selling/auctions/in-the-pajero-evolution-mitsubishi-aimed-a-dakar-legend-at-the-streets/) , and this model won’t upset that apple cart. The new Pajero shares a ladder frame with the Triton mid-size pickup, but Mitsubishi’s engineers put considerable effort into adapting the frame to a three-row SUV layout while also strengthening it. Stronger body mounts help isolate additional road vibrations from the cabin.


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Suspension also plays a key role in adventure-worthiness. The new Pajero employs a double-wishbone independent setup in the front and a newly developed five-link solid axle design with coil springs in the rear. While 9 inches of ground clearance isn’t exactly world-beating, it does beat the[American-market Toyota Land Cruiser](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/first-drive-review-2024-toyota-land-cruiser-is-one-for-the-die-hards/) , which offers 8.7 inches stock.


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi’s Super Select 4WD-II (SS4-II) four-wheel-drive system offers four settings: 2H (rear-wheel drive), 4H (full-time four-wheel drive with an open center differential that allows for differing wheel speeds at either end), 4HLc (four-high with a locked center differential), and 4LLc (four-low with a locked center differential). New for this generation of Pajero, Mitsubishi’s Super-All Wheel Control (S-AWC) integrated vehicle dynamics system will handle side-to-side torque distribution, traction control settings, and the anti-lock brake system.


You’ll get seven drive modes: Normal, Eco, Gravel, Snow, Mud, Sand, and Rock, each adjusting parameters within the S-AWC system to help you make it through whatever’s ahead.


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


Power comes from a 2.4-liter turbodiesel four-cylinder that pairs with an eight-speed automatic transmission. That motor, Mitsubishi says, is good for 201 HP at 3500 rpm and 354 lb-ft of torque from 1750–2500 rpm.


Mitsubishi


Inside, cabin appointments appear fit for the flagship designation. There’s ample tech up front, with a 14.3-inch infotainment display on the dash and a matching screen in front of the driver. The triple-meter cluster, a hallmark of past generations of Pajero, is back, this time displayed digitally on the center screen and renamed to Multi-Meter. You can customize the three gauges to display data such as altitude, temperatures, compass heading, vehicle pitch and roll angles, and the status of the Active Yaw Control system.


Mitsubishi


Though oddly named, the new Pajero’s Multi Around Monitor system will be helpful for adventurers. It stitches together pictures from four cameras mounted around the vehicle with a 3D model of the SUV to display the surrounding terrain and help you avoid (hopefully) bashing your rocker on a large boulder that’s out of view. Many modern SUVs have something similar to this, so we’re pleased to see Mitsubishi getting with the times.


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi


The new exterior is bold and upright, similar to that of Pajeros past—particularly the early first- and second-gen models. Subtle touches such as the bulges on either side of the hood that carry over onto the roof as well as the C-pillar styling meant to evoke the first-gen Pajero’s roll bar make for attractive modern callbacks to yesteryear.


Mitsubishi


Mitsubishi says the new Pajero will be manufactured in Thailand, which is also where it will launch first. Japan and Australia will be the next markets to get a crack at it. Following those three launches, the company plans to sell this stalwart in nearly 100 countries worldwide. Here’s hoping America winds up somewhere on that list down the road.
